options: A query that returns rows in a different order each time it runs
Reading the same row twice and getting two different committed values
Reading a row that has been permanently deleted
Reading another transaction's uncommitted data, which may later be rolled back and so never really existed
questions.explain: A dirty read means you saw an in-flight, uncommitted change — if that change is rolled back, the value you read never actually existed in the database.

questions.q: In the two-session timeline, what does Session B see while Session A's transaction is still open?
options: Session A's uncommitted ListPrice change (9999.00), before Session A commits or rolls back
The original, unchanged ListPrice, because uncommitted changes are always invisible
An error, because Session A's row is locked
NULL, because the row is in an indeterminate state
questions.explain: Under READ UNCOMMITTED, Session B reads Session A's in-progress change immediately, without waiting for a commit.

questions.q: Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
options: SERIALIZABLE only
All four ANSI isolation levels
READ UNCOMMITTED only
READ COMMITTED and everything looser
questions.explain: READ UNCOMMITTED is the one standard level that doesn't require reads to only see committed data; every stricter level prevents dirty reads.

questions.q: What happens to the value Session B read if Session A then runs ROLLBACK TRANSACTION?
options: Session A's rollback fails because Session B already read the data
Session B's read is automatically corrected to the real value
SQL Server raises an error for Session B retroactively
The 9999.00 value Session B saw never actually existed in the committed database
questions.explain: A rollback undoes the uncommitted change entirely — the dirty value Session B saw has no committed history behind it.

questions.q: What table hint produces the same dirty-read-permitting effect as READ UNCOMMITTED for a single query?
options: WITH (NOLOCK)
WITH (ROWLOCK)
WITH (HOLDLOCK)
WITH (SERIALIZABLE)
questions.explain: WITH (NOLOCK) makes that one query skip honoring other sessions' locks, exactly like running under READ UNCOMMITTED.
